newsitem.title: USA: News Corp.'s 24-hour news channel to start Monday.
newsitem.headline: News Corp.'s 24-hour news channel to start Monday.

text.p: Rupert Murdoch's News Corp. Ltd. will introduce its 24-hour all-news channel on Monday, the third entrant in a competitive market that is unlikely to earn profits until the turn of the century.

Audiences for all-news channels are so small that even Cable News Network, the leader in the field, seldom pulls more viewers than a weak broadcast-network situation comedy. In addition, costs are high and Murdoch's Fox News Channel will start while advertisers' spending is near a peak.
Still, industry analysts and officials said Murdoch's new vehicle was likely to pay off in the long run.

"Over the long term, the costs of the Fox News Channel will be amortized over a global business," said Smith Barney analyst John Reidy. "Murdoch will have more faces he can put his news in front of than any other."
Murdoch told reporters on Tuesday he would be delivering Fox News to Latin America, Asia and Europe by the end of 1997.
"Fox News is part of a strategy to create many distribution outlets," said NatWest analyst Gary Farber.
Neither MSNBC, the other new all-news channel owned by Microsoft Corp. and NBC, nor Fox News is expected to break even until after 2000, executives said.
Fox itself is spending more than $100 million on studios, staff and other costs, Fox News Chief Executive Roger Ailes said in an interview.

Beyond that, in an unusual arrangement, Fox has agreed to pay about $10 per subscriber to cable operators to carry the all-news channel, which some analysts said would cost News Corp. hundreds of millions of dollars.

That aggressiveness, like other Murdoch moves in United States in the 1990s, shocked news and entertainment executives and helped prompt the Walt Disney Co. last winter to cancel plans for an all-news channel at its own ABC network.

Several years back Murdoch paid shockingly high fees for the right to broadcast U.S. football games. Rivals predicted Murdoch would lose money but the games were key to luring stronger local stations to Fox from rival networks.

News Corp. also owns 40 percent of British Sky Broadcasting Corp. in Europe, another satellite service in Asia, a stake in a Latin American satellite venture, as well as the Fox Television broadcast network in the United States.
Tele-Communications Inc., the nation's biggest cable operator, has promised 10 million subscribers for Fox News.

Other leading cable operators such as Comcast Corp., and Cablevision Systems Corp., have also signed on to deliver some subscribers. Murdoch said he would have 17 million Fox News subscribers by Monday's launch.

MSNBC has more than 20 million subscribers, or roughly a third of those reached in the United States by CNN, which is owned by Ted Turner's Turner Broadcasting System Inc. and will soon become part of Time Warner Inc. under those two companies' planned $6.5 billion merger.
Some in the industry believe that either MSNBC or the Fox all-news station will survive in the long run, but not both.
"We'll let them slug it out," Comcast President Brian Roberts said at an industry conference last week.
Murdoch, who last week traded insults with CNN founder Ted Turner, has repeatedly complained that CNN and other U.S. television organisations are too liberal.
Ailes said Fox News, with some 16 hours of original programming on weekdays, will be balanced and aim for viewers slightly older than the early-20s audience courted by MSNBC.
In addition to MSNBC and Fox News, several other speciality news channels are readying for launch. Time Warner/Turner and ESPN, a unit of Disney, are both working on sports-news channels.
ITT Corp. and Dow Jones & Co. plan to launch WBIS, a business and sports service in the New York City area, early next year, and may eventually seek wider distribution.
"There are only so many eyeballs out there and this will fragment the audience further," Natwest's Farber said.
